pages.name: Still there?
pages.task: A quick one to start. 2 kg of water warms from 20 °C to 70 °C. Water's [[specific heat capacity]] is 4,200 J per kg per °C. How much energy goes in?
pages.why: Specific heat capacity is the energy to warm 1 kg by 1 °C. So energy = mass × specific heat capacity × rise. The rise is 70 − 20 = 50 °C. So 2 × 4,200 × 50 = 420,000 J, which is 420 kJ.

pages.name: Hotter is not more
pages.text: Temperature tells you how hot something is. Heat is energy moving into or out of it. A 0.25 kg cup of water at 80 °C cools to a 20 °C room. It gives out 0.25 × 4,200 × 60 = 63,000 J, or 63 kJ. A 100 kg tank at 30 °C cools to the same room. It gives out 100 × 4,200 × 10 = 4,200,000 J, or 4.2 MJ. The cup is hotter, but the tank gives out over 60 times as much.

pages.name: Kettle or tank
pages.task: A 2 kg kettle of water is at 90 °C. A 50 kg tank of water is at 25 °C. Both cool to a 20 °C room. Which gives out more heat?
pages.why: The kettle drops 70 °C. It gives out 2 × 4,200 × 70 = 588,000 J, or 588 kJ. The tank drops only 5 °C, but it holds 50 kg. It gives out 50 × 4,200 × 5 = 1,050,000 J, or 1,050 kJ. The cooler tank gives out more.

pages.name: 200 kJ into ice
pages.task: Now put 1 kg of melting ice on a heater. It sits at 0 °C. 200 kJ goes in. What does the thermometer read?
pages.why: Melting 1 kg takes 334 kJ. 200 kJ is not enough to melt it all. So the ice is still melting, and the thermometer stays at 0 °C. Here is one way to picture it. Temperature follows how fast the molecules jiggle. Melting spends the energy on loosening their hold on each other instead.

pages.name: Melting
pages.text: Here is that 1 kg of melting ice on its heater. The graph plots its temperature against the energy put in. For the first 334 kJ the line stays flat at 0 °C. The energy melts the ice instead of warming it. This is called [[latent heat]]. It is energy taken in or given out as a material changes between solid, liquid and gas, with no change of temperature. The heater's power only sets how long it takes. The bar counts it as changing phase.

pages.name: The climb
pages.text: Once the ice has melted, the line climbs. Each kJ warms 1 kg of water by 1 ÷ 4.2, about 0.24 °C. Warming 1 kg from 0 °C to 100 °C takes 420 kJ. The dashed lines show 1 kg and 2 kg. Twice the water shares each kJ, so 2 kg climbs half as steeply. A smaller mass climbs more steeply.

pages.name: Boiling
pages.text: At 100 °C the line goes flat again for 2,260 kJ while the water turns to steam. That is over five times the 420 kJ that warmed it from 0 °C. A 3 kW heater warms 1 kg from 20 °C to 100 °C in 112 s. Then it takes about 12.6 minutes more to boil it away. Water boils at 100 °C at normal atmospheric pressure. Under a different pressure it boils at a different temperature.

pages.name: Five minutes at 100 °C
pages.task: A 3 kW heater runs for 5 minutes on 1 kg of water already at 100 °C. What happens?
pages.answer: It stays at 100 °C, and about 0.4 kg boils away
pages.why: 5 minutes is 300 s. 3 kW for 300 s puts in 900 kJ. Boiling takes 2,260 kJ for each kg. So 900 ÷ 2,260 is about 0.4 kg boiled away. The rest is still water at 100 °C.

pages.name: Two scales
pages.text: A [[kelvin]] is the same size step as a degree Celsius. Only its zero is different. 0 °C is just where ice melts, and plenty of things are colder. The kelvin scale starts at absolute zero, −273.15 °C. So ice at 0 °C is at about 273 K, and it still holds energy. A rise of 100 °C is a rise of 100 K, because the steps are the same size.

pages.task: 2 kg of seawater passes through a cooler each second and warms by 10 °C. Seawater's specific heat capacity is about 3,850 J per kg per °C. How much heat does it carry away?
pages.why: Each second it carries 2 × 3,850 × 10 = 77,000 J. A joule each second is a watt. So it carries away 77 kW.

pages.name: Ice to 100 °C
pages.task: 0.5 kg of ice sits at 0 °C, melting. How much energy turns it into water at 100 °C?
pages.why: Melting 0.5 kg takes 0.5 × 334 = 167 kJ. Warming it from 0 °C to 100 °C takes 0.5 × 4.2 × 100 = 210 kJ. Together that is 377 kJ.
